records.prompt: Explain how shares, bonds, mutual funds and ETFs differ, especially diversification and liquidity. Give a neutral comparison with sources where available.
records.answer:
Model knowledge (not verified against retrieved sources):
A share usually represents an ownership stake in a company. A bond is a loan to its issuer: the bondholder is a creditor, not an owner, and the bond’s terms set out payments and repayment. A conventional mutual fund pools investors’ money into a portfolio; investors own fund units or shares rather than directly owning each security in the portfolio. An ETF is also a fund, but its units are traded on an exchange.

Model knowledge (not verified against retrieved sources):
Holding individual shares or bonds concentrates exposure in those particular issuers. A mutual fund or ETF can spread exposure across many holdings, but the extent depends on what it owns: a narrow fund may still be concentrated, while a broad fund may spread exposure more widely. Diversification can reduce the effect of a poor result from one holding, but cannot eliminate all losses.

Model knowledge (not verified against retrieved sources):
Liquidity is how readily an investment can be bought or sold without a large delay or price concession. Shares and ETFs commonly trade on exchanges during trading hours; an ETF’s exchange price can differ from the value of its underlying holdings, and trading ease depends on market conditions and the holdings’ liquidity. Conventional mutual funds are typically bought from or redeemed with the fund at a price based on its net asset value, rather than traded continuously on an exchange. Bonds vary considerably: some trade readily, while others may be harder to sell quickly or at a favorable price. These are typical mechanisms, not guarantees of sale at a desired price.

The cited guide describes ETFs as investment funds listed and traded on a stock exchange, pooling investors’ money to invest according to the ETF’s stated objective [Guide to ETFs: Understanding Exchange-Traded Funds](https://www.moneysense.gov.sg/guide-to-etfs-understanding-exchange-traded-funds/). It says mutual funds and ETFs provide diversification across a mix of asset classes [A beginner's guide to investing in Singapore](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/infohub/educational-resources/a-beginners-guide-to-investing-in-singapore). An ETF tracking a stock index can provide exposure to that index without investing in all its component stocks [Guide to ETFs: Understanding Exchange-Traded Funds](https://www.moneysense.gov.sg/guide-to-etfs-understanding-exchange-traded-funds/). The guide says designated market makers provide ETF liquidity through continuous bid-ask prices during the trading day; if a market maker fails to perform, liquidity may disappear and selling ETF units may become difficult [Guide to ETFs: Understanding Exchange-Traded Funds](https://www.moneysense.gov.sg/guide-to-etfs-understanding-exchange-traded-funds/).

The cited passages do not explain what investors own in individual shares or bonds, compare mutual funds structurally with ETFs, or compare the buying and selling ease of shares, bonds, and mutual funds. The comparisons below are general descriptions; liquidity varies by security and market conditions.

records.answer:
Zero-based budgeting is a way to plan where all of your expected income will go. Assign every amount a purpose—such as bills, everyday spending, savings, or debt payments—until planned income minus planned outflows equals zero. This does not mean spending everything: savings and debt payments can be purposes too. Start with expected income, list expenses and commitments, assign the remaining amount to priorities until none is unassigned, then review and adjust the plan as circumstances change.

records.prompt: Explain mutual funds and ETFs as two numbered options, in that order, and compare how they work.
records.answer:
1. Funds

Model knowledge (not verified against retrieved sources):
A conventional mutual fund pools money from many investors to hold a portfolio of investments. Investors own shares or units in the fund, and the fund’s value per share or unit is generally calculated from the portfolio’s net asset value (NAV). Purchases and redemptions are typically processed at a price based on a once-daily NAV. Unlike an ETF, a conventional mutual fund is not generally bought and sold on an exchange throughout the trading day.

2. Exchange-traded funds

Model knowledge (not verified against retrieved sources):
An exchange-traded fund (ETF) pools investors’ money in a portfolio, but its shares trade on an exchange during the trading day, much like a listed share. Its market price can change during the day and may differ somewhat from the portfolio’s NAV. Both conventional mutual funds and ETFs can hold diversified portfolios; the main practical difference is that conventional mutual fund transactions are typically priced using a daily NAV, while ETF trades occur at exchange prices during the day.
